screens.title: The Mediator Pattern: Centralizing Communication
screens.subtitle: Coordinate interactions through a single mediator to reduce coupling and clarify flow.

narration.text: In this lesson we will study the Mediator pattern and why it matters for system design. Many systems grow tangled because objects talk directly to many others. That creates tight coupling and a maintenance burden when requirements change. The Mediator pattern solves this by routing communication through a central component. Think of an air traffic controller: planes report to the tower, and the tower coordinates movements so planes do not need direct references to each other. In software, colleagues send messages to a mediator, which encapsulates routing and coordination rules. You will see the pattern’s structure — mediator interface, concrete mediator, colleague abstraction, and concrete colleagues — and a runnable Java example using a chat room. We’ll also look at a traffic intersection starter activity where the mediator decides whether cars proceed based on a light’s state. Pay attention to the trade-off: the mediator centralizes complexity, so its responsibilities must be focused to avoid a god object. By the end you’ll be able to decide when a mediator reduces coupling and how to keep it maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Route colleague interactions through a focused mediator to reduce pairwise coupling and contain coordination logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will build and verify

narration.text: These objectives guide our practice with the Mediator pattern. First, you will understand the core problem: many objects with direct links leads to tangled dependencies and maintenance pain. You will learn to identify that smell in code and explain why a mediator helps. Second, you will implement the Mediator pattern in Java. That means writing a mediator interface, a concrete mediator, an abstract colleague, and concrete colleagues, and wiring them so colleagues only communicate via the mediator. Third, you will learn to recognize scenarios where the Mediator improves maintainability, such as chat rooms, GUI dialogs, and traffic simulations, and how it reduces pairwise references. Fourth, you will compare direct communication and mediator-based designs, understanding the trade-offs: reduced coupling at the cost of concentrated coordination logic. Each objective includes practical checks: small tests, examples to run, and a competency milestone to verify the skill. We will use concise code snippets and a traffic-light starter to practice. By the end you should be able to decide when to introduce a mediator and how to avoid common pitfalls like creating a god object.

screens.title: The problem: tangled direct communication and tight coupling
screens.subtitle: Why many-to-many references become a maintenance hazard

narration.text: Large systems often reveal the same structural problem: objects needing to interact with many peers create a web of direct links. This web increases coupling because each object must know interfaces and behaviors of multiple other objects. A change in one object may require changes in all objects that reference it, producing the ripple effect that makes refactors risky. A common symptom is scattered interaction logic across many classes; each class contains code to notify or update peers. That makes it hard to understand the flow of messages and to write isolated tests for a single component. The Mediator pattern addresses this by moving the interaction logic out of colleagues and into a mediator. The mediator becomes the single place where routing and coordination rules live. A helpful way to think about this is the air traffic control analogy: planes do not coordinate directly, the controller does. One misconception is that centralizing always reduces complexity; it does not. Centralizing moves complexity into one component deliberately, and that component must be sized and scoped carefully. The key question to ask is whether moving coordination into a mediator makes the overall system easier to reason about and maintain, or merely hides complexity behind another interface.

keyIdea.title: Problem statement
keyIdea.text: Many-to-many direct references scatter interaction logic and cause tight coupling; a mediator centralizes coordination to reduce pairwise dependencies.

content.html:
Core Concept
Tangled direct communication
When objects hold references to many peers, update and notification logic appears in multiple places, making the codebase fragile and hard to reason about.
  • Symptoms: many imports, long constructors with peer parameters, duplicated routing logic.
  • Why it matters: changes ripple across peers, tests need many collaborators instantiated.
  • Misconception: direct communication is always simpler — it can cause long-term maintenance costs.
Analogy: Air traffic control
Planes report to a central tower that coordinates takeoffs and landings, so each plane doesn't need to know the state of every other plane.
Diagram: many-to-many vs mediator
Direct links
Multiple arrows between objects. Interaction logic sprinkled across classes.
Mediator
One central arrow to mediator that routes messages and coordinates behavior.
Key Takeaway

Move coordination to one focused component only when it reduces overall coupling and improves clarity.

screens.title: What the Mediator pattern is
screens.subtitle: A behavioral pattern that encapsulates interactions in one object

narration.text: The Mediator pattern defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. In formal terms, colleagues hold a reference to the mediator and notify it when their state changes or when they need to request an action. The mediator knows its colleagues and performs the necessary routing logic, invoking colleagues' methods or broadcasting messages. This promotes loose coupling because colleagues are no longer aware of each other; they only know the mediator's interface. A concrete mediator implements coordination rules specific to that interaction context. One concrete example is a chat room mediator: users send messages to the chat room, and the chat room broadcasts to other users or routes private messages. A misconception is that mediator removes all complexity — instead it concentrates coordination logic so designers should ensure the mediator has narrowly focused responsibilities. If coordination needs cross many unrelated concerns, split into multiple mediators. A useful diagnostic is to ask whether introducing a mediator reduces the total number of distinct dependencies across the team of classes, and whether changes will be localized to the mediator instead of spread across many colleagues.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A mediator centralizes interaction rules so colleagues communicate only through a single interface, reducing pairwise coupling.

content.html:
Definition
Mediator: central coordinator
Colleagues notify the mediator and the mediator coordinates responses and routing of messages to other colleagues.
Colleague role
Holds a mediator reference and delegates communication to it instead of to peers.
Mediator role
Implements coordination rules and knows its colleagues so it can route or broadcast messages.
Concrete example
ChatRoom mediator
Users send messages to ChatRoom which broadcasts to other users. Adding a new user touches the ChatRoom only.
Common mistake
Giving the mediator unrelated responsibilities turns it into a god object.

screens.title: Pattern structure: interface, mediator, colleague, concrete colleagues
screens.subtitle: Common elements you implement in Java

narration.text: The Mediator pattern typically contains four elements you should implement explicitly. First, the mediator interface defines methods colleagues use, such as sending messages and registering participants. For example, a chat mediator may offer sendMessage and addUser. Second, the concrete mediator implements that interface and holds references to colleagues. It performs the routing and coordination logic for the collaboration. Third, the colleague abstraction — an abstract class or interface — holds a reference to the mediator and defines send and receive methods. Fourth, concrete colleagues implement the colleague interface and focus on their own state and behavior, delegating communication to the mediator. This separation keeps colleagues lightweight and focused. When implementing in Java, the mediator maintains a collection of colleagues and iterates to broadcast or selectively notify. Watch for concurrency and for the tendency to make the mediator aware of too many unrelated types. If you need to coordinate several domains, design multiple mediators or split responsibilities so the Single Responsibility Principle still holds. Always keep an eye on testability: mediators are natural places for integration tests, while colleagues become easier to unit test because they use the mediator interface rather than concrete peers.

keyIdea.title: Structure
keyIdea.text: Implement a mediator interface and concrete mediator, plus colleague abstraction and concrete colleagues that use the mediator for communication.

content.html:
Architecture
Pattern elements
  • Mediator interface: defines communication methods colleagues call.
  • Concrete mediator: holds colleagues, routes messages, and implements collaboration rules.
  • Colleague abstraction: stores mediator reference and declares send/receive.
  • Concrete colleague: implements behavior and delegates interaction to mediator.
Design notes
Mediator keeps the collaboration rules; colleagues remain small and easier to test. Use multiple mediators when interactions span unrelated domains.
Example roles
ChatMediator, ChatRoom (concrete mediator), User (colleague), ChatUser (concrete colleague).

screens.title: Implementing the mediator interface and colleague abstraction
screens.subtitle: Java interfaces and abstract classes that shape collaboration

narration.text: Let's walk through the first code pieces you will write: the mediator interface and the colleague abstraction. The mediator interface declares operations colleagues use, for example sendMessage and addUser in a chat scenario. This interface is intentionally simple so colleagues depend only on an abstraction. Next, create an abstract colleague class that stores a protected mediator reference and a name. It defines abstract send and receive methods that concrete colleagues implement. This design keeps the colleague focused on behavior and state while delegating interaction to the mediator. A common concrete implementation uses a constructor that accepts the mediator and registers the colleague with the mediator as needed. One important implementation detail is avoiding tight coupling to the concrete mediator type: depend on the mediator interface. Also consider lifecycle: who creates the mediator and who registers colleagues? The mediator often is created by the client code and colleagues receive the mediator reference at construction time. A misconception to avoid is putting business logic for routing in each colleague; routing belongs in the mediator so changes to message flow are localized. Implementing the mediator interface and colleague abstraction means depend on the mediator interface from colleagues and implement send/receive in concrete colleagues; keep routing logic in the mediator.. In practical terms, java interfaces and abstract classes that shape collaboration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Coding rule
keyIdea.text: Depend on the mediator interface from colleagues and implement send/receive in concrete colleagues; keep routing logic in the mediator.

content.html:
Code: mediator
<!-- ChatMediator.java -->
interface ChatMediator {
  void sendMessage(String message, User user);
  void addUser(User user);
}

<!-- User.java (abstract colleague) -->
abstract class User {
  protected ChatMediator mediator;
  protected String name;

  public User(ChatMediator mediator, String name) {
    this.mediator = mediator;
    this.name = name;
  }

  public String getName() { return name; }
  public abstract void send(String message);
  public abstract void receive(String message);
}
Notes
  • Keep the mediator interface minimal and focused on communication operations.
  • Make colleagues depend on the interface, not a concrete mediator class.
  • Register colleagues with the mediator during construction or via a separate registration call.
Key Takeaway

Design the mediator interface first so colleagues code against abstraction and routing stays centralized.

screens.title: Concrete mediator and colleague: ChatRoom and ChatUser
screens.subtitle: How the mediator holds colleagues and broadcasts messages

narration.text: Now examine the concrete mediator and colleague implementations from the chat example. The concrete mediator holds a collection of colleagues, typically a list. When addUser is called the mediator stores the colleague. When sendMessage is invoked, the mediator iterates the list and forwards the message to all colleagues except the sender. The concrete colleague implements send and receive: send delegates to mediator. sendMessage, and receive handles incoming messages locally, for example printing to a console. This design centralizes message routing in the mediator and keeps the colleague focused on its local behavior. A practical detail to watch for is avoiding sending messages back to the sender unless desired. Also consider concurrency: if multiple threads call sendMessage concurrently, the mediator's collection must be thread-safe or synchronized. A common misconception is to let colleagues know about other colleagues' concrete types; do not. The mediator should be the only place that knows about the set of participants. When you run the chat demo, you will see console output showing each user receiving messages from others, demonstrating the mediator’s role. Concrete mediator and colleague: ChatRoom and ChatUser means the concrete mediator stores colleagues and routes messages; concrete colleagues delegate sends and handle receives locally.. In practical terms, how the mediator holds colleagues and broadcasts messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concrete roles
keyIdea.text: The concrete mediator stores colleagues and routes messages; concrete colleagues delegate sends and handle receives locally.

content.html:
Concrete Mediator
// ChatRoom.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class ChatRoom implements ChatMediator {
  private List<User> users;

  public ChatRoom() { this.users = new ArrayList<>(); }

  @Override
  public void addUser(User user) { this.users.add(user); }

  @Override
  public void sendMessage(String message, User sender) {
    for (User user : this.users) {
      if (user != sender) {
        user.receive(sender.getName() + " says: " + message);
      }
    }
  }
}
Concrete Colleague
// ChatUser.java
class ChatUser extends User {
  public ChatUser(ChatMediator mediator, String name) { super(mediator, name); }

  @Override
  public void send(String message) {
    System.out.println(this.name + " sending message: " + message);
    mediator.sendMessage(message, this);
  }

  @Override
  public void receive(String message) {
    System.out.println(this.name + " received message: " + message);
  }
}

screens.title: Run the chat demo and observe message flow
screens.subtitle: Client wiring and console output that proves the mediator routes messages

narration.text: Run the client code to see how the mediator acts at runtime. The client constructs the concrete mediator, creates concrete colleagues with a mediator reference and optional registration, and then invokes send on colleagues. Each send call delegates to the mediator, which forwards the message to other participants. Watch the console output: the sender logs that it sent a message, and each recipient logs receiving the message along with the sender's name. This runtime trace is the best way to verify the mediator is in control: no colleague calls methods on other colleagues directly. A misconception is to assume registration is optional; if the mediator does not know its colleagues, it cannot forward messages. Design the registration step so it is explicit or automatic in the colleague constructor. Also keep an eye on ordering and delivery guarantees: if you need strict ordering or durability, the mediator must implement these policies. Finally, use unit tests that mock the mediator interface to exercise colleague behavior in isolation and integration tests to validate the mediator's routing logic. screens.title: Trade-offs: loose coupling vs mediator complexity
screens.subtitle: When centralizing helps and when it can harm

narration.text: Applying the Mediator pattern reduces pairwise coupling but concentrates coordination logic. The main benefit is maintainability: colleagues are simpler, have fewer dependencies, and are easier to test in isolation. Adding a new colleague typically requires changes only in the mediator rather than in every existing colleague. The downside is that the mediator can grow large and assume too many responsibilities. This creates a god object that is difficult to understand and modify, and potentially a single point of failure. To evaluate whether the mediator is appropriate, ask two questions: does centralizing interactions reduce the total number of links and make the collaboration rules clearer, and can the mediator's responsibilities be scoped to a cohesive domain? If interactions span unrelated concerns, prefer multiple mediators or a different pattern. Another trade-off involves performance and concurrency: the mediator may become a bottleneck depending on routing policies and synchronization. A common mitigation is to partition responsibilities into smaller mediators and keep coordination policies narrow. Always document the mediator’s responsibilities so future maintainers know where to look for interaction logic. Trade-offs: loose coupling vs mediator complexity means use mediators to simplify coupling when responsibilities are cohesive; split mediators if coordination diversifies into unrelated concerns.. In practical terms, when centralizing helps and when it can harm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: Use mediators to simplify coupling when responsibilities are cohesive; split mediators if coordination diversifies into unrelated concerns.

content.html:
Benefits
  • Reduced coupling between colleagues.
  • Single place to change routing and coordination rules.
  • Colleagues become easier to unit test.
Risks
  • Mediator can become a god object if responsibilities expand too far.
  • Potential single point of failure and performance bottleneck.
  • Concurrency concerns when multiple threads interact with mediator state.
Mitigations
Design mediators with narrow, cohesive responsibilities; split coordination into multiple mediators if needed; make collections thread-safe or synchronize access; and write integration tests to validate routing logic.
Pro-tip

Document the mediator’s scope in code comments and design notes so teams avoid adding unrelated logic later.

screens.title: When to apply Mediator: practical scenarios
screens.subtitle: Practical signs that a mediator will help maintenance

narration.text: Look for clear signs that suggest a mediator will help. First, when an interaction involves many components with interdependent updates — for example, a chat room with many users or a complex dialog where multiple UI controls update each other — a mediator can centralize those rules. Second, when adding a new participant currently requires edits across several classes: if adding one object touches many peers, a mediator can localize the change. Third, when coordination logic needs to be changed frequently, placing it in a mediator reduces the number of classes to edit. A concrete GUI example: a text box, a button, and a list box where text changes enable the button and list selection updates the text box. Without a mediator, each component needs references to others. With a dialog mediator, components notify the mediator and it enables or populates controls as appropriate. A common misconception is that mediator is a silver bullet for all coupling; it is best used when interactions are cohesive and domain-specific. Ask whether the mediator would simplify reasoning and reduce tests that need many collaborators. If yes, it is a good candidate.

keyIdea.title: When to choose
keyIdea.text: Apply the mediator when interactions are many-to-many and cohesive, and when it reduces the total spread of change across classes.

content.html:
Scenario
GUI coordination
TextBox notifies DialogMediator when content changes. Mediator decides whether to enable Button or update ListBox.
Scenario
Chat routing
Users send messages to ChatRoom which broadcasts or routes to specific recipients.
Assessment example
If a TextBox, Button, and ListBox directly reference each other, the design suffers tight coupling. A DialogMediator coordinates enabling and populating behavior so components only know the mediator.

screens.title: TrafficLightMediator starter walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Guide to implement the intersection mediator in the starter code

narration.text: The starter activity asks you to implement a TrafficLightMediator coordinating Car and TrafficLight colleagues. Begin by defining an IntersectionMediator interface with methods to register cars and lights, and methods to notify that a car arrived or a light changed. The provided abstract colleagues—CarColleague and TrafficLightColleague—already hold a mediator reference and define methods like arriveAtIntersection, proceed, waitAtIntersection, changeColor, and isGreen. Implement ConcreteIntersectionMediator so it keeps a reference to the current traffic light and a queue or list of waiting cars. When a car arrives and the light is green, the mediator tells the car to proceed. When the light is red, add the car to waitingCars and tell it to wait. When the light changes to green, iterate over waitingCars and signal them to proceed, removing them from the list. Consider iteration safety: iterate over a copy of the list or remove items carefully to avoid concurrent modification. This exercise practices moving decision logic (canProceed?) out of cars and traffic lights and into the mediator, showing how the mediator coordinates multiple colleague types within a focused domain. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Starter steps

  2. Implement ConcreteIntersectionMediator with a TrafficLight reference and waitingCars list.
  3. On carArrived: if light.isGreen(), call proceed(); otherwise call waitAtIntersection() and add to waitingCars.
  4. On lightChanged to GREEN: iterate over a copy of waitingCars, call proceed(), and remove each.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and how to avoid a god object
screens.subtitle: Recognize and mitigate the mediator becoming too powerful

narration.text: A frequent pitfall when using the Mediator pattern is allowing the mediator to become a god object. This happens when unrelated coordination tasks are accumulated in one mediator, or when business logic not related to routing is placed in the mediator. The result is a class that is hard to test, understand, and change. To avoid this, apply the Single Responsibility Principle: the mediator should coordinate a cohesive set of colleagues for a specific collaboration. If you find the mediator contains code for multiple domains, split it into smaller mediators, each responsible for one domain. Another pitfall is over-generalization: making the mediator too generic with conditionals for many colleague types. Prefer clear, explicit mediator methods for the collaboration you need. Also be mindful of concurrency and lifecycle: mediators that manage registrations and collections must handle concurrent arrivals and removals safely. Finally, avoid hiding state changes without clear contracts; ensure the mediator exposes enough behavior via its interface to write meaningful unit tests and integration tests that validate coordination policies. Common pitfalls and how to avoid a god object means keep mediators focused. split responsibilities, avoid over-generalization, and design for testability and safe concurrency.. In practical terms, recognize and mitigate the mediator becoming too powerful. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoiding anti-patterns
keyIdea.text: Keep mediators focused. Split responsibilities, avoid over-generalization, and design for testability and safe concurrency.

content.html:
Pitfall
God object
Mediator accumulates unrelated logic and becomes difficult to maintain.
Pitfall
Over-generalization
Too many conditionals for many colleague types hides the collaboration intent.
Pitfall
Concurrency and lifecycle
Unsynchronized collections or unclear registration lead to runtime problems.
Mitigation

Refactor mediators by responsibility, document the mediated collaboration, add integration tests for routing, and choose thread-safe collections or synchronized access when necessary.

screens.title: Design and testing tips for robust mediators
screens.subtitle: Practical advice to keep mediators maintainable and testable

narration.text: Use these practical guidelines when implementing mediators. First, design the mediator’s public A P I before colleagues so colleagues depend on a stable abstraction. Keep methods descriptive and limited to the coordination tasks needed. Second, prefer composition over inheritance for colleagues when you need flexible behavior. Third, write unit tests that mock the mediator interface to verify colleague-specific behavior without involving routing code. For mediator tests, write integration-style tests that register multiple colleagues and assert routing and delivery outcomes. Fourth, avoid mutable global state inside the mediator; prefer instance-level state with clear lifecycle management. Fifth, if multiple coordination contexts exist, split mediators rather than expand one. A final tip relates to concurrency: if the mediator manages a list of colleagues accessed by multiple threads, use thread-safe collections or synchronize access where necessary. These practices help ensure the mediator simplifies the system rather than transferring maintenance cost to a single unwieldy class. Design and testing tips for robust mediators means design the mediator api first, test colleagues by mocking the mediator, test mediator routing with integration tests, and avoid global mutable state.. In practical terms, practical advice to keep mediators maintainable and testable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical tips
keyIdea.text: Design the mediator API first, test colleagues by mocking the mediator, test mediator routing with integration tests, and avoid global mutable state.

content.html:
Design tips
  • Define mediator API first; colleagues program to the interface.
  • Keep mediator methods focused and descriptive.
  • Split mediators when interactions cover multiple domains.
Testing & concurrency
  • Unit-test colleagues by mocking the mediator interface.
  • Integration-test mediator routing with multiple colleagues registered.
  • Use thread-safe collections or synchronization for concurrent access.
Key Takeaway

A well-designed mediator simplifies collaboration only when its API, responsibilities, and tests are deliberately defined and enforced.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core terms and their concise meanings

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important terms. The Mediator Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that encapsulates how related objects interact by introducing a central coordinator. The Mediator is an interface that defines operations colleagues use to communicate, like sending messages or registering participants. The Concrete Mediator implements those operations and contains the routing logic and references to colleagues. These definitions form the vocabulary you will use when designing and discussing mediator-based solutions. Remember: the goal is to reduce direct references between colleagues by routing communication through a mediator, but keep the mediator tightly scoped so it does not turn into a god object. Try to explain each term in one sentence to a peer — that quick rehearsal helps cement understanding. Key Concepts — Part 1 means mediator centralizes interactions; mediator interface defines communication; concrete mediator performs routing and holds colleagues.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick summary
keyIdea.text: Mediator centralizes interactions; mediator interface defines communication; concrete mediator performs routing and holds colleagues.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts
Mediator Pattern
An object that encapsulates interactions among a set of objects, reducing direct references.
Mediator
An interface defining communication methods colleagues call to coordinate actions.
Concrete Mediator

A colleague is an object that participates in a mediated interaction; it holds a mediator reference and delegates communication to that mediator. A concrete colleague implements behavior such as sending and receiving messages and relies on the mediator for coordination. Loose coupling is the design goal: colleagues avoid direct knowledge of peers, making the system easier to change and test. Remember the design trade-off: the mediator contains coordination logic, so keep its responsibilities narrow and consider multiple mediators if interactions span different domains. content.html:
Colleague
An object that delegates communication to the mediator and focuses on its own state.
Concrete Colleague
An implementation that sends requests to and reacts to notifications from the mediator.
Loose Coupling
A design goal where components have minimal dependencies on each other, improving maintainability.
Takeaway

Map the chat and traffic examples to these roles to practice identifying mediator, concrete mediator, colleagues, and the benefits of loose coupling.
